# On the Word "Ampolla"

A single noun can hold within it a surprising multiplicity of meanings, and the word "ampolla" is a fine example of this richness. It names, first of all, a disease that afflicts the peach tree, curling and swelling its leaves. But it also describes the tender blister that rises on human skin after an injury—that small, fluid-filled dome that forms without necessarily breaking open. Beyond these, the word extends itself further still, reaching toward the deformations found in plants and even in metals, wherever a surface bulges and lifts away from itself. To follow the word is to trace a common thread of swelling and rupture across the boundaries of the living and the inert.

For me, the word summons a specific memory from childhood, when I was perhaps five or six years old. There was a man who lived on Alabama Street, in the house that stood next to Saint Peter's. I can still picture him clearly, dressed in a starched white t-shirt, its stiffness somehow inseparable in my mind from the man himself.

On the occasion I remember, he brought out a gun to show me. I suppose he assumed—correctly—that a child of my age had never seen such a thing up close, let alone held one in his own hands. There was a kind of pride in the gesture, the pride of an adult introducing a young person to an object of consequence.

But I handled it clumsily, as any child would. In my inexpert grip, the hammer of the gun pressed down and dug into the fleshy base of my thumb. The skin did not break. Instead, a swelling rose there, tight and filled with fluid—an ampolla in the most literal sense, a blister born of that small, unremarkable violence.

It is curious how the word carries other resonances too. The Spanish "ampolla" connects, through its history, to the medieval crystal ampul—the small sealed vessel that might once have held the blood of a holy person, preserved as a relic. There is something fitting, perhaps, in this echo: a vessel of blood held safely behind a thin transparent wall, much like the swelling on my thumb. And the gun, I should add, was almost certainly not loaded—though the memory of it, sealed within me all these years, remains as vivid as any relic.

# Blister

**blister** *(n.)* 1. A raised portion of the epidermis, filled with serous fluid, resulting from friction, burning, or other injury to the skin.

I keep returning to that word, the way it holds so many wounds inside its two syllables. There is the blister that rises on a leaf—**2.** *a diseased swelling on plant tissue*—the tomato vines curling in July heat, their surfaces pocked and blighted, the way rust travels through the garden until nothing green remains untouched. And there is the blister of the sea vessel—**3.** *a protective bulge or armored compartment on the hull of a warship*—that swelling built precisely to absorb what would otherwise pierce and sink. As though the body knew, always, to rise up where it feared the deepest harm.

I was young. There was a man—older, though I could not have told you then whether older meant thirty or sixty—who lived in a low house on Alabama Street. The screen door, the smell of cut grass and something underneath it, something metallic. He put the gun in my hands the way you might hand a child a stone, expecting me to know its weight without instruction.

I remember the hammer.

I remember pulling it back, and the way it caught the meat of my thumb, the pad of it, and pressed. A small pain. A rising. Later I would look and find the skin swollen there, tender, a blister raised by pressure alone—no fire, no friction, only the sustained insistence of metal against the softest part of me.

*A raised portion. A protective bulge. A diseased swelling.*

The language keeps trying to tell me something. That the body swells to shield itself. That danger leaves its architecture on the skin. That memory itself is a kind of blister—the mind's fluid gathering beneath an injury, cushioning the place where something struck.

I have carried this for years believing it was the story of how close I came. The gun, the thumb, the older man, the afternoon light coming sideways through the screen.

And only now, saying it aloud, do I understand the worst part, the part that unsettles more than any narrow miss:

it probably wasn't even loaded.

# Ampolla

**blister**, *n.* — a small bubble on the skin filled with serum, caused by friction, burning, or other damage to the tissue beneath.

The metal was colder than I expected, colder than the creek in April where my brother dared me to stand until my ankles went numb. Grandfather's hands over my hands. *Like this.* The weight of it pulling my wrists down toward the earth.

**ampolla**, *f.* — ampolla. Del latín *ampulla*: frasco pequeño, redondo. A little flask. A vessel meant to hold.

What I remember is not the sound but the space where sound should have been, the way the afternoon folded around it and did not open again. Cicadas resuming their argument in the pecan trees. My palm already announcing itself.

**blister** — *v.* to become covered in blisters; to speak harshly, to scorch with words: *a blistering rebuke.*

He said nothing. That was the thing. He looked at where the can had been and did not say *good* and did not say *again* and the silence was its own instruction, hot along the meat of my thumb where the trigger had pressed its small red catechism.

**ampulla** — also: a rounded sac or dilation in a canal or duct of the body. A widening. A place where the vessel swells to hold what moves through it.

My mother pressing the needle to a match. *You have to let it drain or it fills again.* The way she held my hand open like something she was reading. All that clear water risen up beneath the skin, translucent, a lens over the tender new pink that wasn't ready yet, that the world had reached anyway.

**blister** — from Middle Dutch *bluyster*, a swelling. Compare Old French *blestre*.

I was seven. I want to say I understood the gravity, the way a life could be halved by less pressure than it takes to open a screen door. But I understood only the sting, the bubble rising like a small clear country between me and everything I had touched, the body doing what it does: putting water between the wound and the air.

**ampolla** — a bubble. A blister. A little flask. The vial the venom comes in and the vial the cure. The same word. The same rounded swelling. Something held apart, briefly, from the thing that would enter it.

*Like this,* he said. And the field went quiet. And my hand kept the shape of it for days.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

# CHARGE

**charge** (v.) *to rush forward in attack*

The dog came at me low and fast when I was six, and I have never forgotten the geometry of it—the way a body can become a straight line aimed at yours.

**charge** (n.) *the price asked for goods or services*

My father asked what it would cost to make me unafraid. The trainer named a figure. My father, who counted every dollar twice before releasing it into the world, wrote the check without counting.

I did not know then what a thing that was.

**charge** (v.) *to entrust with a task or responsibility*

*I charge you*, my mother said, *to look after your brother.* I was eight. He was four. This is how the oldest child learns that love is a form of custody, that to be given something precious is also to be made liable for its loss.

**charge** (n.) *an accusation, especially a formal one before a court*

The charge against me, when I finally faced it, was this: that I had spent thirty years managing everyone's fear and none of my own. There was no judge. There didn't need to be. Some verdicts arrive without ceremony.

**charge** (n.) *a quantity of electricity*

Here is what they don't tell you about the body: it runs on the same current as lightning. That when you are afraid, something in you is literally *charged*, held at a potential, waiting for the ground.

My brother, all those years I watched him, was always waiting for the ground.

**charge** (v.) *to fill or imbue*

The room was charged, we say, when we mean nobody spoke and everybody understood. My family specialized in charged rooms. We could fill a silence so completely that words would have been a kind of vandalism.

**charge** (n.) *the amount an explosive device is loaded with*

A charge is also what you set when you intend to bring something down. A controlled demolition. My therapist called it that—*a controlled demolition*—when I finally decided to tell them the truth about who I was, what I wanted, whom I loved.

You set the charge. You clear the building. You accept that what stood there will not stand again.

**charge** (v.) *to restore energy to a depleted battery*

But the same word. That is the thing I keep returning to. The same word for the thing that destroys and the thing that restores. To charge is to attack and to charge is to replenish. My father wrote the check to make me brave and my mother made me a guardian and both of them were, in their way, charging me—loading me, depleting me, filling me back up.

**charge** (n.) *a person placed in someone's care*

My brother is forty now. He calls me on the bad nights. I am still, it turns out, his charge—or he is mine, I have never been sure which direction the word points, whether I hold him or he holds me at the end of that telephone line, two charged bodies waiting for the same ground.

**charge** (v.) *to move toward, fast, without stopping*

The dog. I want to end with the dog.

What the trainer taught me, with my father's uncounted money, was this: you do not run from the thing that charges you. You turn. You face the straight line of it. You make yourself the ground it was always racing toward.

I have been turning to face it my whole life.

I am not finished.

I am still charged.

counterfactuals.output:
# Ampolla

*or, the many ways a thing can rise*

---

**I. Plant Disease**

On the leaves of the peach tree, *ampolla* means the blister rust, the curl, the way a leaf remembers water it should not have held. My mother called it *la ampolla* and cut the branch. She said some things swell because they are sick, and some things swell because they are trying to survive, and you cannot always tell which by looking.

The old man on Alabama Street had a peach tree that never fruited. He said it was too proud to give anything up. I was seven and did not know that a tree could be both dying and refusing to die at the same time. I know it now.

---

**II. Skin Swelling**

*Ampolla:* the pocket of fluid that lifts the skin from itself. A small architecture of hurt. The body building a room around an injury.

His hands were full of them—old blisters gone to callus, the kind you get from seventy years of holding tools that were hotter or heavier than they should have been. He let me press my thumb into his palm and feel where the skin had thickened into something that no longer registered pain.

*This is what happens,* he said, *when you keep touching the thing that burns you.*

I did not ask what the thing was. On Alabama Street you learned not to ask. You learned that some blisters are the story, and some blisters are only the scar tissue of a story already told and buried.

---

**III. Ship Blister**

In shipbuilding, *ampolla* is the bubble of air trapped beneath the paint, beneath the hull's skin, where damp got in and could not get out. Left alone, it spreads. Left alone, the water underneath keeps working, quiet, patient, rusting the iron you cannot see.

His house was like that. Beautiful from the street—white paint, a porch, the illusion of a hull that could still take water. But inside, the walls had risen in places, paint lifting from plaster, and when you pressed them they gave like something soft, something wet, something that had been holding weather for decades and telling no one.

He lived inside the blister. He was the trapped air and the slow rust both.

---

**IV. Aircraft Compartment**

The *ampolla* of a plane: the glass bubble, the cockpit dome, the transparent blister where the gunner sat exposed to all that sky. A swelling made of clarity. A place you climb into knowing you can be seen from every direction, knowing the thing that protects you is also the thing that shows you to the world.

He flew, once. Or he said he flew. On Alabama Street the difference between a man's memory and a man's mercy on himself was not something children were allowed to measure. He described the ampolla, the plexiglass, the cold, the way the earth looked like a body under a sheet.

*You could see everything from up there,* he said, *and everything could see you. That's the trade. That's the only trade there ever is.*

---

**V. Medieval Reliquary**

And then the oldest meaning: *ampolla,* the small glass vessel, the phial, the swelling of blown glass that held the blood of a saint, the oil, the water from a holy place. A blister made on purpose. A swelling built to carry something worth keeping.

When he died, they found the house full of them. Not saints' blood. Buttons. A daughter's first tooth. A wedding ring gone green. A photograph of a woman whose name no one on Alabama Street had ever heard him say. Each one sealed in its own small container, its own swelling of intention, its own architecture built around a hurt he had decided to keep.

I understand it now, the way I did not at seven:

A blister is the body's confession that something got inside.
A blister is the proof that you were touched.

He spent his whole life rising around the things that entered him—the burns, the water, the sky, the woman—and calling each swelling by a different name so that no one would know it was all the same wound, lifting the same skin, building the same holy room around the same unspeakable relic.

*This is what happens when you keep touching the thing that burns you.*

You become the reliquary.
You become the glass that holds the blood.

---

You become the many ways a thing can rise.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

# Cleave

*v. to split; also, to cling*

---

From Old English *clēofan*, to divide—
and *clifian*, to adhere.

The same tongue,
two hungers.

---

My mother in the kitchen,
knife against the cutting board,
halving something
that resisted.

*A word that means itself
and its own undoing.*

---

I learned it young:
how to be split
and how to hold.

The screen door hung
by one hinge, swinging—
*to part, to stay.*

---

Consider the axe.
Consider the marriage vow,
*to cleave unto*—

the way she said his name
like pressing a bruise
to see if it still hurt.

---

I was seven, maybe eight.
The distinction between
*coming apart*
and *coming together*
was a hallway
I stood in the middle of.

---

Etymologists call this
a *contronym*—
a word divided
against itself,
each meaning
a room with the light off.

---

Downstairs, their voices:
the long dividing,
the terrible adhering.

I pressed my palm flat
to the cool plaster wall
as if to hold the house
in one piece—

*clifian*, to cling—

or feel it
split.

---

What I remember:
the knife, the board,
the thing that resisted,
finally
giving.

Whether it opened
or was joined—

I have spent
the rest of my life
not knowing
which.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
